sectionToMerge.h2: Frequently Asked Questions About Robotic Gastrectomy for Gastric Cancer
sectionToMerge.intro: Robotic gastrectomy is a minimally invasive way to remove part or all of the stomach for gastric cancer using a surgeon-controlled robotic system. These FAQs explain how it works, who may be suitable, recovery, cost, and access for international patients.

items.q: What is robotic gastrectomy for gastric cancer?
items.a: Robotic gastrectomy is a minimally invasive surgery to remove part or all of the stomach for gastric cancer using a robotic system controlled entirely by the operating surgeon. The surgeon sits at a console and guides tiny instruments through small incisions with a magnified 3D view. It aims to remove the tumour and nearby lymph nodes with precision. Whether it suits a patient depends on cancer type, stage, and specialist review.

Robotic gastrectomy works through a few small incisions rather than one large cut. The surgeon controls robotic arms from a console, using wristed instruments and a high-definition, magnified 3D camera to remove the affected stomach tissue and lymph nodes. The digestive tract is then reconnected. The robot does not operate on its own; every movement is directed by the surgeon. Suitability and technique depend on tumour location, stage, and the treating team's assessment.

items.q: How is robotic gastrectomy different from laparoscopic or open surgery?
items.a: Robotic gastrectomy differs from laparoscopic and open surgery mainly in the tools and view the surgeon uses. Compared with open surgery, both robotic and laparoscopic approaches use small incisions and may allow faster recovery. Robotic systems add wristed instruments and magnified 3D vision, which can help with precise lymph node removal and reconstruction. The best approach depends on tumour stage, location, surgeon experience, and should be discussed with the treating team.

items.q: What types of gastrectomy can be performed robotically?
items.a: Robotic techniques can be used for several types of gastrectomy, including subtotal (partial) gastrectomy, total gastrectomy, and in some centres proximal gastrectomy. The choice depends on where the tumour sits, its stage, and how much stomach must be removed to achieve clear margins and adequate lymph node clearance. Not every tumour is suited to a robotic approach, so the final decision is made by the surgical oncology team after full assessment.

items.q: Who is eligible for robotic gastrectomy?
items.a: Robotic gastrectomy may be suitable for selected patients with gastric cancer that can be removed surgically, often earlier-stage or locally advanced tumours judged operable. Eligibility depends on cancer type, stage, tumour location, previous treatment, body build, prior abdominal surgery, and overall fitness for anaesthesia. Some advanced or bulky tumours may be better treated with open surgery or other approaches. A qualified oncology and surgical team decides suitability after reviewing scans, endoscopy, and biopsy results.

items.q: What tests are needed before robotic gastrectomy?
items.a: Before robotic gastrectomy, patients usually need staging and fitness tests to plan surgery safely. These commonly include upper endoscopy with biopsy, CT scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis, and sometimes PET-CT or diagnostic laparoscopy to check tumour spread. Blood tests, nutritional assessment, and heart and lung evaluation help confirm fitness for anaesthesia. The exact tests depend on the individual case and should be guided by the treating oncology and surgical team.

items.q: How long does robotic gastrectomy take and what is recovery like?
items.a: Robotic gastrectomy typically takes several hours, and recovery varies by patient and the extent of surgery. Many patients begin walking within a day or two and gradually restart fluids and soft foods as the digestive system heals. Hospital stays are often a few days to about a week. Full recovery, including adjusting to smaller meals, can take weeks to months. Recovery times are estimates and depend on individual healing and specialist advice.

items.q: What are the benefits of robotic gastrectomy?
items.a: Robotic gastrectomy may offer benefits such as smaller incisions, less blood loss, reduced pain, and potentially faster recovery compared with open surgery in selected patients. The magnified 3D view and wristed instruments can help surgeons remove lymph nodes and reconstruct the digestive tract with precision. These are potential advantages, not guarantees, and cancer control still depends on stage and completeness of removal. The benefit for any individual should be discussed with the surgical team.

items.q: What are the risks or side effects of robotic gastrectomy?
items.a: Robotic gastrectomy carries risks similar to other major stomach surgery, including bleeding, infection, blood clots, and leakage where the digestive tract is rejoined. Longer-term effects can include changes in eating, weight loss, dumping syndrome, and vitamin deficiencies needing supplements. Conversion to open surgery is sometimes necessary. Serious complications are uncommon but possible. Risks vary by patient and should be discussed in detail with the treating surgical and oncology team before deciding.

items.q: Is robotic gastrectomy safe for all gastric cancer patients?
items.a: Robotic gastrectomy is not suitable for every gastric cancer patient, though it is considered safe in appropriately selected cases. Patients with very advanced tumours, extensive spread, certain prior surgeries, or who are not fit for prolonged anaesthesia may be better served by other approaches. Safety depends on cancer stage, overall health, and the surgical team's experience. Final decisions about whether this operation is appropriate should be made by the treating medical team.

items.q: How much does robotic gastrectomy cost?
items.a: The cost of robotic gastrectomy varies widely by country, hospital, and individual case, so a single fixed price cannot be quoted. Final cost depends on the hospital, diagnosis, stage, tests, surgical protocol, length of stay, any complications, and the treating team's advice. Robotic surgery can cost more than open or laparoscopic surgery because of the technology involved. Patients should request a detailed, personalised estimate from the treating hospital before planning treatment.

items.q: Which countries offer robotic gastrectomy for gastric cancer?
items.a: Robotic gastrectomy is available in many countries with advanced cancer centres, including parts of Asia, Europe, and North America, as well as select hospitals in India and China. Availability depends on whether a centre has robotic systems and surgeons trained in gastric cancer surgery. Because expertise and outcomes vary between centres, patients considering treatment abroad should confirm the hospital's experience with this specific procedure and discuss options with their oncology team.

items.q: Is robotic gastrectomy available in India?
items.a: Robotic gastrectomy is available at several major cancer and multi-speciality hospitals in India that have robotic surgical systems and trained gastrointestinal cancer surgeons. Availability and experience differ between centres, and not every hospital offers it for stomach cancer. Costs in India are often lower than in some Western countries, which attracts international patients. Whether it is appropriate still depends on the individual diagnosis, stage, and assessment by the treating surgical team.

items.q: Is robotic gastrectomy combined with chemotherapy or other treatments?
items.a: Robotic gastrectomy is often part of a wider treatment plan rather than a standalone cure. Depending on stage, patients may receive chemotherapy before surgery to shrink the tumour, or chemotherapy and sometimes radiotherapy afterwards to reduce recurrence risk. The surgery removes the tumour, while other treatments address microscopic disease. The exact combination depends on cancer type, stage, biomarkers, and response, and should be planned by a multidisciplinary oncology team.

items.q: Are there clinical trials involving robotic gastrectomy?
items.a: Yes, some clinical trials study robotic gastrectomy, often comparing it with laparoscopic or open surgery for outcomes such as recovery, lymph node removal, and long-term results. Trials may have strict inclusion and exclusion criteria, and eligibility is decided only after medical record review and investigator assessment. Taking part does not guarantee benefit or enrolment. Patients interested in trials should discuss available options and their suitability with their treating oncology team.

items.q: Can robotic surgery be used for advanced or recurrent gastric cancer?
items.a: Robotic surgery may be considered for some locally advanced gastric cancers, but its role in very advanced or recurrent disease is more limited and carefully selected. Extensive tumour spread, involvement of nearby organs, or scarring from previous treatment can make a robotic approach less suitable, and open surgery or non-surgical treatments may be preferred. Whether surgery of any kind is appropriate in advanced or recurrent cases must be decided by the treating medical team.

items.q: How can international patients access robotic gastrectomy?
items.a: International patients can access robotic gastrectomy by first sharing their medical records for review, then obtaining an opinion and treatment plan from a hospital experienced in gastric cancer surgery. Access depends on hospital acceptance, medical review, visa approval, fitness to travel, and the patient's condition. None of these can be guaranteed in advance. Planning usually involves cost estimates, appointment scheduling, and arranging follow-up care, ideally coordinated with the patient's home oncology team.

items.q: What medical reports are needed to plan treatment abroad?
items.a: To plan robotic gastrectomy abroad, patients usually need to provide key medical reports for review before travel. These commonly include the endoscopy and biopsy results, pathology reports, recent CT or PET-CT scans, blood test results, and a summary of any previous treatment. Complete and up-to-date records help the surgical team assess suitability and give a more accurate plan and estimate. The treating hospital may request additional tests after reviewing the initial reports.

items.q: How does CancerFax help patients with robotic gastrectomy?
items.a: CancerFax helps patients organize medical reports, identify relevant specialists or treatment centers, estimate possible costs, and coordinate second opinions, appointments, travel, visa, and follow-up support. Treatment decisions are always made by the qualified oncology team after reviewing the patient's diagnosis, stage, biomarkers, previous treatment, and overall health. This support is intended to guide and coordinate care, not to guarantee hospital admission, visa approval, or any particular treatment outcome.
